title: Code of Good Practice for Milk Producers in the dairy industry

lessons.title: Purpose and principles of the code
lessons.html:
Why the dairy industry has a code

Milk is a food that reaches almost every household, including babies and the elderly. The public expects it to be safe, produced humanely and without harming the environment. A single serious incident, such as antibiotic residues or contamination, can damage trust in the whole industry. The South African dairy industry's Code of Good Practice for milk producers sets out the practices that responsible producers follow, so that processors, retailers and consumers can trust raw milk from the farm.

How the code relates to law and buyer standards

  • The code builds on legal requirements; it does not replace them. Where the law sets a requirement, the farm must comply regardless of the code.
  • Milk buyers and retailers often have their own supplier standards based on similar principles and may audit farms against them.
  • The code also includes good practice beyond the legal minimum, for example in animal welfare and environmental care.

Core principles

  1. Food safety: milk free from harmful bacteria, residues and contaminants.
  2. Animal health: prevention-based herd health with veterinary involvement.
  3. Animal welfare: animals free from hunger and thirst, discomfort, pain, injury and disease, fear and distress, and able to express normal behaviour.
  4. Feed and water: safe, traceable feed and clean water.
  5. Environment: responsible use of water, soil and chemicals, and proper waste management.
  6. People: safe, fair and lawful working conditions with appropriate training.
  7. Traceability and records: evidence of what was done, to whom and when.

Key legislation

Foodstuffs, Cosmetics and Disinfectants Act 54 of 1972 (food safety); Act 36 of 1947 (feeds and stock remedies); Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962; Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984; National Water Act 36 of 1998; Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983; OHS Act 85 of 1993; Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997.

lessons.title: Requirements in key areas
lessons.html:
Milk hygiene and food safety

  • Hygienic milking routine and clean, maintained milking equipment.
  • Rapid cooling and temperature records.
  • Clean, separate milk room protected from pests.
  • Clean water of potable quality for cleaning milk-contact surfaces.
  • Staff hygiene: clean clothing, hand washing, no milking when ill with a transmissible condition.

Medicines and residues

  • Use registered veterinary medicines and stock remedies, prescribed or used according to the label.
  • Identify treated animals and keep their milk out of the supply for the full withdrawal period.
  • Keep a treatment register and secure medicine storage.
  • Dispose of sharps and expired medicines safely.

Animal health and welfare

  • A written herd health plan with the farm vet.
  • Prompt treatment of sick and injured animals; humane euthanasia where needed.
  • Adequate feed, water, shade and shelter; comfortable lying areas; good walkways.
  • Calm handling, without beating or unnecessary use of electric prodders.
  • Painful procedures done by trained persons with pain relief as advised by the vet.
  • Calf care, including colostrum for every calf and humane treatment of bull calves.
  • Fitness for transport of animals leaving the farm.

Feed and water

  • Feed from reliable suppliers, with records.
  • Safe storage to prevent mould, pests and chemical contamination.

Environment

  • Effluent contained and used or disposed of without polluting water resources.
  • Safe storage and disposal of chemicals and containers.
  • Responsible water use and soil conservation.

People

  • Compliance with labour law and fair labour practices.
  • Risk assessment, protective equipment and training on hazards such as chemicals, machinery and animals.
  • First aid facilities and trained first aiders.

lessons.title: Compliance, auditing and the producer's responsibility
lessons.html:
Who is responsible?

The milk producer, the owner or person in charge of the farm, is responsible for compliance. In practice, the dairy unit manager plans and checks the systems, supervisors run them daily, and every worker carries out the procedures. Everyone must understand what the code requires of their job.

Building a compliance system

  1. Know the requirements: the code, the law and the buyer's standard.
  2. Assess the farm with a checklist and identify gaps.
  3. Write procedures (SOPs) for key tasks: milking, cleaning, treatment, calf care, chemical handling.
  4. Train staff and keep training records.
  5. Keep records that prove compliance.
  6. Monitor and review regularly.

Audits

TypeDescription
Internal (self) auditDone by the farm's own team using a checklist
Second-party auditDone by the milk buyer or processor
Third-party auditDone by an independent certification or inspection body

During an audit, the auditor observes practices, interviews workers and examines records. Findings are classified, for example as major or minor non-conformances, and the farm must submit corrective actions within an agreed time.

Risk-based thinking

Focus effort where the risk is highest. Residues, contamination and serious welfare or safety failures carry the greatest consequences. Identify what could go wrong at each step, how likely it is, how serious it would be, and what control prevents it. This is the same logic as HACCP-based food safety systems used by processors.

Benefits of compliance

  • Secure milk contract and access to premium markets.
  • Fewer losses from rejected milk, disease and injuries.
  • Better herd health and productivity.
  • Protection of the industry's reputation.

Key points

  • The code builds on SA law and covers food safety, health, welfare, feed, environment, people and records.
  • The producer is responsible, but every worker must understand their part.
  • Use SOPs, training, records and monitoring to show compliance.
  • Audits may be internal, by the buyer, or independent.
  • Focus on the highest risks, especially residues and contamination.
